name: The van 't Hoff Equation
statement: The van 't Hoff equation states that d(ln K)/dT equals the standard reaction enthalpy divided by RT², linking equilibrium-constant shifts to temperature.
meaning: The equation quantifies how a reaction’s equilibrium constant K changes with temperature, given the standard enthalpy change of the reaction. Exothermic reactions have K decrease with rising temperature, endothermic reactions have K increase. Plotting ln K against 1/T (a "van ’t Hoff plot") gives a line whose slope yields the reaction enthalpy and whose intercept yields the reaction entropy.
mechanism: The relation follows from combining the definition of the equilibrium constant via ΔG° = −RT ln K with the Gibbs–Helmholtz equation relating ΔG° and ΔH°. Integrating over a temperature range, assuming the reaction enthalpy is approximately constant, gives ln(K2/K1) = −(ΔH°/R)(1/T2 − 1/T1).

examples.text: Plotting ln K versus 1/T from equilibrium constants measured at several temperatures and reading the slope and intercept is a standard method to extract the reaction enthalpy and entropy.
The equation is applied to critical-micelle-concentration data, treated as an equilibrium constant, to determine the thermodynamics of surfactant micelle formation.

It is used to predict how the equilibrium constant for a dissolution or gas-solubility equilibrium shifts with temperature, consistent with Le Chatelier’s principle for exothermic and endothermic processes.

whyItMatters: It provides a quantitative, thermodynamically grounded bridge between reaction enthalpy and the temperature-dependence of chemical equilibria, letting chemists predict equilibrium shifts and extract thermodynamic parameters from temperature-varying equilibrium data without independent calorimetry.
limits: The commonly used integrated form assumes the reaction enthalpy (and implicitly entropy) is constant over the temperature interval, which is only an approximation since both vary with temperature via heat-capacity differences; it is most accurate over narrow ranges.
misreadings: A frequent misreading is treating the integrated form as exact over wide temperature ranges, when it is strictly valid only under the constant-enthalpy approximation.
origin: Proposed by Dutch chemist Jacobus Henricus van ’t Hoff in 1884 in his book "Études de Dynamique chimique."

sources.text: Van ’t Hoff equation, Wikipedia. — the differential and integrated forms, the 1884 origin, the constant-enthalpy approximation, and the van ’t Hoff plot.
